name: Common carp aquaculture at Jiahu, Henan
summary: People at the Neolithic village of Jiahu in Henan, China, were raising common carp in managed waters by about 6000 BCE, according to a study of fish bones.
description: A 2019 study of fish bones from prehistoric East Asia argues, from the ages at which fish died and the species chosen, that common carp were being raised under management at the Early Neolithic site of Jiahu, Henan Province, by around 6000 BC. The claim rests on bone profiles, not on remains of ponds, and the study does not show that later Chinese carp farming descended from it.

impact.note: Raising fish instead of only catching them was a new capability, but it is shown for one Neolithic community and its region, and no later fish farming is shown to descend from it.

date.label: by c. 6000 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Managed aquaculture of common carp was present at the Early Neolithic Jiahu site, Henan Province, China, by around 6000 BC.

evidence.supports: was present at the Early Neolithic Jiahu site, Henan Province, China, by around 6000 bc

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Only the abstract was read; the full paper should be opened for which Jiahu period the managed carp belong to.
The lead's subject, historical carp pond farming (the treatise attributed to Fan Li, about 500 BCE), was not researched, and continuity from Jiahu to it is not shown.
Egyptian and Mesopotamian fish ponds were not checked, so whether Jiahu is the earliest aquaculture anywhere is open.

research.note: The study dates managed carp at Jiahu but does not compare it with other regions, so whether it was the earliest anywhere is not established.
